summary: This informational document describes principles of traffic engineering in the Internet, to improve understanding of the issues and give a common basis for developing capabilities. It covers architectures and methods for evaluating and optimizing operational networks. It first appeared as RFC 3272 in 2002, and this revision obsoletes that document.

eli5.summary: Traffic engineering is like planning roads so that cars spread out and nobody gets stuck. This is the basic guidebook for doing that on the internet.

questions: what are the elements of traffic engineering
subtitle: The shared vocabulary and principles for steering traffic through IP networks so they stay fast, reliable and not overloaded.

tldr.problem: Operators need to measure and shape how traffic uses their networks, but traffic engineering spans many techniques and terms that had no common frame of reference.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terminology and a repeating process of policy, measurement, analysis and optimization, classifies TE systems on seven axes, surveys IETF techniques, and gives recommendations.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3272, a 2002 document, updating it with current practice and later IETF work. It is informational and sets no protocol rules.

today: RFC 9522 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 3272, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It describes principles and practice rather than a protocol.

sections.title: What Traffic Engineering Is
sections.content:
Internet traffic engineering (TE) is the part of network engineering that deals with performance evaluation and performance optimization of operational IP networks. It covers measuring, characterizing, modeling and controlling traffic, and its central job is steering traffic from ingress nodes to egress nodes.

What matters is performance as end users see it: delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput. TE reaches this through capacity management (planning, routing control, resource management) and traffic management (conditioning, queue management, scheduling). It can be proactive, such as engineering backup paths, or reactive, such as rerouting after a failure.

The focus is TE inside one domain such as an Autonomous System, with a short look at inter-domain TE. The RFC was first published as RFC 3272 in May 2002 and is a complete update of it; around three-fifths of the RFCs it references postdate RFC 3272.
sections.eli5: Traffic engineering means watching how busy the roads are and steering cars onto the best routes, both before and after trouble happens.

sections.title: The Three Elements of a TE Solution
sections.content:
The RFC says any TE solution needs some aspect of three elements, and solutions with only some are "partial TE".

  • Policy chooses paths using more than basic reachability. BGP is a common way to apply it; the policies themselves are left to the network operator.
  • Path steering forwards packets using more than the next hop. Examples named are IPv4 source routes, RSVP-TE explicit routes, Segment Routing and Service Function Chaining.
  • Resource management controls bandwidth, buffers and queues. Reservation is the control-plane side (admit, reject or reclassify a flow); allocation is the data-plane side (buffers, policing, rate shaping).

The terminology section also defines terms such as congestion, hotspot, traffic flow, traffic trunk, traffic matrix and offered load, so that the rest of the document is precise.
sections.eli5: You need rules about who may go where, a way to actually send cars down a chosen road, and a way to save room on that road.

sections.title: Congestion and How to Fight It
sections.content:
A resource is congested when traffic arriving exceeds its output capacity over an interval. A little congestion at the network edge can be useful for keeping links full, but network congestion raises delay and delay variation, may cause loss and makes services less predictable. Fighting it at reasonable cost is a major objective of TE.

The RFC sorts congestion management three ways. By timescale: long (weeks to months, adding capacity), medium (minutes to days, adjusting routing parameters or LSPs) and short (minutes or less, such as queue management with Random Early Detection and Explicit Congestion Notification). By approach: reactive or preventive. By side: supply-side (add or rebalance capacity) or demand-side (regulate the offered load through policing and rate shaping).
sections.eli5: If a road is jammed you can build more road, send cars another way, or let fewer cars on at once. Which one you pick depends on how fast you need the jam cleared.

sections.title: The TE Process and a Taxonomy of Systems
sections.content:
TE is an iterative process of four phases repeated continually: define control policies, acquire measurement data, analyze network state and workload, and optimize performance. Measurement, modeling and optimization are its key components, and optimization can be corrective (fix a problem) or perfective (improve without a problem).

Section 4 classifies TE systems along seven contrasts: time-dependent, state-dependent or event-dependent; offline or online; centralized or distributed; local or global; prescriptive or descriptive; open-loop or closed-loop; tactical or strategic. In practice most systems are hybrids. For example, a popular MPLS approach pairs a central Path Computation Element controller with local decisions made by routers using routing and signaling protocols.
sections.eli5: Engineers keep repeating a cycle: decide the rules, look at the traffic, work out what is wrong, and then fix it. There are many styles of doing this, such as one boss or every router deciding alone.

sections.title: Techniques and Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 5 reviews IETF mechanisms that support TE, including Integrated Services, Differentiated Services, MPLS, RSVP-TE, GMPLS, IP Performance Metrics, TE extensions to the IGPs, BGP-Link State, the Path Computation Element and Segment Routing, along with content distribution.

Section 6 gives recommendations. They cover generic non-functional qualities (such as automation), routing, traffic mapping, measurement, policing and planning, network survivability, multi-layer TE, Diffserv environments and network controllability. On survivability it recommends a philosophy of robustness, and names tools such as MPLS Fast Reroute. Section 7 notes that with BGP the outbound exit point is controllable but the inbound point generally is not, and most TE policy follows a "closest exit" strategy.
sections.eli5: The guidebook lists the tools engineers already have, and gives advice such as having backup roads ready and checking regularly how busy things are.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC calls TE mechanisms security neutral and says it introduces no new security issues, then lists trade-offs. Tunnels can help hide traffic and can be encrypted, and TE can steer traffic through more secure links or security-function nodes. On the other side, predictable paths may be easier to find and attack, and extra complexity can lead to errors.

Attacks on TE control protocols could hijack traffic, steer it onto poor paths or congest key links, so authentication should be used on all TE protocols. External control interfaces risk exposing a network's internals and must be secured and authenticated. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Steering traffic can make it safer or easier to target. Whoever controls the signposts must be properly checked, or they could send cars the wrong way.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PHASES OF THE TE PROCESS MODEL (REPEATED CONTINUALLY)

items.title: 1. Define policies
items.text: Set the control policies that govern how the network operates.

items.title: 2. Acquire measurements
items.text: Collect measurement data from the operational network.

items.title: 3. Analyze
items.text: Characterize workload and network state, proactively and reactively.

items.title: 4. Optimize
items.text: Choose and apply actions to control offered traffic and its distribution.
